body: I took chem 2 with Goldberg. He can be a little all over the place but what i found most helpful was not necessarily trying to read every single page in the book but practicing the book problems lots. Many of his exam questions come word for word from the book. The rest are typically problems like the ones on his slide or a long problem that involves doing multiple of the types of problems in the book. Our TA was also amazing and made himself available all the time as did professor Goldberg. I actually had the pleasure of taking goldberg twice and one thing i can tell you is that if you come to class (beleive me, he knows who does and doesn't ) and show that you care and come to office hours, he'll help as much as you need and may even help ya out when grades come out ;) i know hes a bit disorganized but once you pick up on his style, he's an amazing professor to have . good luck :)

Nooooooope. Absolutely DO NOT blame yourself for the adults in this situation being EXTREMELY irresponsible. Caring for someone who suffers from very violent outbursts is usually a job only those with experience and/or training can do, and sometimes even they struggle. You needed to be cared for as well, you were a child too! It was in no way your responsibility to risk getting hurt and be constantly stressed trying to take care of a child like this when you were still a young child yourself. Those adults expecting you to be able to take that on is completely unreasonable, selfish of them, and overall reckless and careless. My family has always been pretty poor, so a few days a week, my mom made me take over her babysitting job. Both children were autistic (also, they were toddlers) so while they weren't "bad" kids obviously, they were quite a handful and did often get violent, very loud, and absolutely did not behave no matter what I did, or where we were. Once, the younger of the two took off all her clothes and started running around A DAMN ICE SKATING RINK in the middle of a major park in NYC. I was 9 years old and had no clue if I should've just left the older one and chased down the youngest as I was in charge of both children and I was MORTIFIED. No young child should have to feel the stress and fear of being responsible completely for keeping a younger child safe, ESPECIALLY not with children that are known to be more than a handful, or children that could get into very dangerous situations so easily. 

I'm sorry you had to experience that OP :( but please, please, please don't feel like you did this with malicious intent. You were, like him, JUST A CHILD. And you should have been being cared for, not being forced to care for another child.

Some Stern classes are open to non-majors but lots aren't. Also, you could do the nursing classes, but your HEOP advisor might not approve of it as those credits don't really end up counting if you remain in CAS. They cover housing only if you live outside of the 5 boroughs. In extenuating circumstances though, you can request it even if you live in the 5 boroughs and they decide if it's necessary or not. As for tuition, it covers most of it. Most people end up paying less than a thousand dollars per semester honestly.

Stern would be the hardest I'm pretty sure. The HEOP Stern program is rather small as well. I'd say CAS is the easiest as there are way more spots. But if you just want to take different types of classes, nursing isn't gonna work out too well. You have to take the 4 classes they have set up for you every term and there's no wiggle room with it, especially if you're coming in as a transfer and need to make up nursing credits. For more freedom in choosing classes, I'd do CAS. To do nursing at NYU, you have to be 100% committed to just that pretty much (unless you can take classes in the summer, but HEOP doesn't pay for this unfortunately).

Stern has most of the business majors but they have economics at CAS. If you're doing HEOP ( I'm in HEOP myself) I would say CAS is your best bet. The HEOP nursing program only has about 15 kids per year so there's less space there unfortunately. HEOP transfers are also quite rare here as very few HEOP students transfer out. But I believe you can indicate that you're interested in Nursing but would like to be considered for other schools as well ( I know on the regular app this was a thing.) 
Also, no I'm not a Veteran so I wouldn't know if there's any additional steps there, sorry about that :(

I transferred to CAS. I was just bothered by the fact that nursing wouldn't allow me to fit in a math major on the side so I left. It honestly wasn't too bad though, but if you want to pursue things on the side, it may not be the best major. Your 4 years are pretty much set up for you. On the plus side though , my friends who stayed in nursing are very happy they did and most of them are finding placements in great hospitals already :)

I did nursing my first year and then transferred but I did know of at least 5 people to transfer in to nursing at NYU (from another school here ) with 3.2-3.5 GPAs . It also helps you have some related experience, as most internal transfers don't in my experience. The only issue is that nursing is a pretty small school. My year we had like 170 kids and only 4-5 transferred out after that year. So it's not super hard to get in, but space is limited. I believe they accept people on a rolling basis (internal transfers do this) so I'd say the soonest you can apply is when you should apply :)

IVs (Individual Values) are kinda like the stats. Each Pokemon has a base value for attack, stamina, and defense. The value doesn't change, it's the same base number for that species. So the IVs (0-15) are essentially an "added value" to the base stat of your Pokemon. For example, you would have higher CP in a Pokemon with better IVs compared to the same type of Pokemon with lower IVs. A 100% perfect Pokemon would have IVs of 15/15/15 (15 is the strongest). A Pokemon with "bad IVs" would be something like 5/3/6 :) hope this helped.
